Q: Type casting char pointer to be of type struct pointer A:

To focus on the question in your title: You can cast an array of char or unsigned char¹ to any other type, so long as the buffer has at least the right size and at least the right alignment. (An array of signed char would work too, but no one ever does that.) You may want to consistently use char buffers to hold strings and unsigned char for bytes of untyped data.

C always counts object sizes as a number of char (even on machines that can address individual bits). This means that, to fill a buffer with any larger object, you need to increment it by the size of the object. And EVENT_SIZE is defined to be sizeof (struct inotify_event). In this case, it appears that an inotify_event struct can contain bytes of extra data at the end, and that how many is stored in its len field. That appears to be the reason why the loop is filling an array of char instead of struct inotify_event, and why it increments the current position by EVENT_SIZE + event.len.

Language-Lawyery Update

Although this is a bit more into the weeds than you need right now, I have to address it. There are a number of incorrect answers and comments claiming that there is some kind of undefined behavior from strict aliasing. (If that were true, I don’t see how it would be possible to write an arena allocator in C, as that inherently requires reinterpreting bytes within a buffer as some other effective type.)

The C23 Standard §6.5.1(6) says (adding emphasis to the clauses relevant to your example, which are not about objects of no declared type):

If a value is copied into an object having no declared type using memcpy or memmove, or is copied as an array of character type, then the effective type of the modified object for that access and for subsequent accesses that do not modify the value is the effective type of the object from which the value is copied, if it has one. For all other accesses to an object having no declared type, the effective type of the object is simply the type of the lvalue used for the access.

So there are two situations where the effective type is copied along with the object: either using memcpy or memmove into an object with no declared type, or when the object is copied as an array of character type. There is a comma between the parallel clauses here. The main verb is repeated in both. It is completely unambiguous. Does the sentence, “If the meeting ends at 6:00, I’ll be home for dinner, or if the meeting ends later than that I won’t be home in time,” mean that I will only miss dinner if the meeting ends at 6 o’clock sharp? Several people in the comments sound like they think it does. The sentence structure is exactly the same!

Additionally, §6.2.6(4) states that copying the object into an array of unsigned char preserves its object representation, that this is “the addressable storage unit holding it,” and that two values with the same object representation (other than NaN) compare equal. So you can definitely dereference the pointer and take the value.

Since this code sample copies the the struct as an array of character type, the effective type is set correctly, and the pointer alias is legal (next paragraph, first item). There is one other potential source of undefined behavior: casting a misaligned pointer is undefined behavior. I don’t think this would be an issue with this type, but best practice is to declare a buffer you will use to store some other type of data with alignas or _Alignas.

Even if a compiler that didn’t allow this very common idiom could declare itself conforming to some people’s interpretation of the language standard, no actual compiler does and any compiler that did would break on a lot of existing code, so it’s nothing you need to worry about.

Copying with memcpy() will work in more cases and perform as well, so it’s good advice.

Q: How do I make a 'for' loop in python run infinitely? A:

for is meant to perform an action for all items of a concrete container. If you need something to just keep running, you should be using the while statement instead.

Note that while it is easy to create an infinite generator, or an infinite iterable in Python which could be used to drive an infinite for loop, (1) it would be semantically incorrect; (2) the most readable and straightforward ways to create an infinite gerator will themselves use a while construct.

That said, here is an inifinite iterable which doesn't create more objects at each iteration, and doesn't use a while loop, by creating an object which is iterable, and which just returns anything when iterating, without checking any boundaries:

class InfiniRun:
     __iter__ = lambda(self): self
     __next__ = lambda(self): None

for i in InfiniRun():
    ...

Q: "Windows uses UTF-16 as its internal encoding", what exactly does this mean? A:

On the other hand, suppose Windows uses ASCII as its internal encoding, does this mean that any applications on it can never display Chinese characters correctly?

If the system only supports ASCII then any application wanting to display non-ascii characters would have to do so without the help of the OS.

But systems that only support ASCII. What was far more common is systems where values in the range 0-127 were ASCII while values in the range 128 to 256 had meanings that varied from one locale to another.

These encodings can be divided into two categories, in "single byte" encodings each byte represented a single character, in "multi byte" encodings some characters required a sequence of multiple (usually two) bytes.

no matter C, C++,.NET or Java

Programming languages do matter, because they play a strong role in determining how programs handle strings internally and how they interact with the OS.

this application will get data from a remote machine

There are critical questions of how it gets that data, what if any processing it does to that data, and how it passes the data to the OS.

Windows uses UTF-16 as its internal encoding", what exactly does this mean?

It means that the format for string data inside NT-based windows, is UTF-16.

However, that does not mean UTF-16 is the only encoding used. Windows also uses "legacy" encodings. Typically there are two legacy encodings in play.

  • The "ANSI" codepage (1252 on English locales).
  • The "OEM" codepage (437 on American systems, 850 on other English locales).

Most windows API functions come in two versions. The "w" versions take UTF-16 strings, while the 8-bit versions take strings made up of bytes. Most of the "a" functions work in the "ANSI" codepage, but there are some situations where the OEM codepage is used.

Many older windows applications use the "a" APIs. So the character encoding these applications use to interact with the OS depends on what locale the OS is configured for.

So for example, consider two Simplified Chinese users are chatting using an old IRC client that uses the "a" APIs. An English user of the same IRC client is trying to watch the conversation.

One of the Chinese users types their Chinese text, windows internally handles this text in UTF-16, but the old IRC client is using the "a" APIs, so windows converts the text to CP936.

The old IRC client doesn't know or care what the bytes outside the ASCII range means, it just passes them to the IRC server. The IRC server doesn't know or care what they mean either, it just passes them to the other users IRC clients.

The other IRC clients pass the data back to the OS using the "a" APIs. However, this turns out differently for the English user and the Chinese user.

The Chinese user's system is expecting code page 936 from the IRC client, so the Chinese text is correctly converted back to UTF-16 and displayed correctly.

The English user's system on the other hand is expecting code page 1252, so when it tries to convert the string back to UTF-16, it uses the wrong encoding resulting in "mojibake".

A more modern IRC client on the other hand, may use the W APIs to retrieve UTF-16 from the OS. The IRC client will need to convert the text to a sequence of bytes to send them to the IRC server, but the client application is now in control of that process. It can choose what encoding it used to encode the bytes sent to the IRC server, and how to interpret the bytes that are returned, either decoding them with a fixed encoding or using some heuristics to guess what encoding they are in.

Some protocols (sadly not IRC) have metadata fields to allow the encoding to be specified, avoiding the need for auto-detection.

Q: pre-receive hook to block no-verify A:

If your concern is AI coding agents (like Claude Code) bypassing hooks, check out block-no-verify. It adds a PreToolUse hook that prevents the agent from running git commit --no-verify entirely. Note: this is agent-specific and not a general server-side solution.

Q: Compare Match A & B IRQs raised at the same time when matches are close to each other A:

I discussed this matter on simavr repository issues section: https://github.com/buserror/simavr/issues/570

The most plausible explanation seems to be that compare match A and B IRQ flags, when set during sleep or executing long (>1 cycle) instruction (which incidentally would be added from that infinite loop from my edit of the question), would be seen from MCU perspective as both set at the same time. Even though compare match B flag was in reality set first, since MCU doesn't check on IRQs until it leaves sleep / finishes executing instruction, during that time compare match A flag would also be set, literally on next clock cycle. And when MCU finally checks on IRQs, both events have their flags raised already. Simavr probably reflects this behavior by only setting IRQ flags when MCU starts to look at them, and that's why they seem to be set at exact same moment in simulator traces.

Q: Return value type of class member accessor function to provide access to vector of unique_ptrs A:

Well "string" is special because it does SSO (small string optimization) - I assume your profiling probably tested against strings that fit into the internal storage, so it ends up doing a very efficient fixed-size stack-copy of memory, and no expensive heap allocation.
If you end up copying something like, 3mb-large strings on each return (or, realistically, any character-limit over the SSO capacity), you will see a very clear degredation of performance. For vector, you should rarely see a benefit by copying, over passing by value (maybe for very small vectors, with trivial types, if you are using a very efficient global allocation library; but not if you have to do a system-heap allocations or copying any expensive types).

;TL;DR always be careful what you are profiling.

The idea isn't all bad though, there are historically cases of developers passing trivial types like "int" by const&, as what you describe as "premature optimization" - which is really a pessimissation. But the modern solution for complex types is returning a view-like container, like string_view or span (by value of course.) This gives you the best of both worlds - value semantics, but no potentially expensive copies.
